title: How the Claude Code harness works
goal: Understand what happens between typing a prompt into Claude Code and a change landing in your repository: the loop, the tools, the permission check, the context, and the places where you can extend it.

includes: The agent loop: the model proposes tool calls, the harness runs them, and the results go back into the context
The permission check, the context and memory files, and the extension points: hooks, subagents, MCP servers, and skills
excludes: Anything the public Claude Code documentation does not state, such as the system prompt text and the exact compaction rules
Settings, flags, and version differences, which change often. Check the current documentation before you rely on a detail

components.label: You and your prompt
components.summary: You type a task. You can also answer permission questions, press Esc to stop, and type a correction while Claude works.
components.explanation:
You are part of the loop, not only the start of it.

- You can **interrupt** at any point with `Esc`.
- You can type a correction while Claude works. Claude reads it after the current tool calls finish.
- You decide what the permission check asks you.

references.label: How Claude Code works
references.path: Claude Code docs: How Claude Code works

components.label: Agent loop
components.summary: Repeats three phases until the task is done: gather context, take action, verify the result.
components.explanation:
The harness asks the model what to do next. The model answers with a tool call or with a final reply. The harness runs the tool, adds the result to the context, and asks again.

The documentation describes the phases as **gather context**, **take action**, and **verify results**. They blend together, and the loop ends when the task is complete or you stop it.
outputs: Tool calls to check and run

references.label: How Claude Code works
references.path: Claude Code docs: How Claude Code works

components.label: The Claude model
components.summary: Reads the context and proposes the next step: a tool call, or a final answer. It does not run anything itself.
components.explanation:
The model reasons about your task and decides which tool to use. The harness provides the tools and manages what the model sees.

The model only **proposes**. Nothing happens on your machine until the harness runs the call.

references.label: How Claude Code works
references.path: Claude Code docs: How Claude Code works

components.label: Context and memory files
components.summary: Everything the model can see now: the conversation, file contents, command output, system instructions, and your CLAUDE.md files.
components.explanation:
**CLAUDE.md files** hold instructions you write once, such as build commands and conventions. Claude Code loads them at the start of every session. Claude treats them as **context, not enforced rules**, so a rule that must always hold belongs in a hook or a permission rule. Claude Code also keeps auto memory, which are notes that Claude writes itself.

The window has a limit. When it nears the limit, Claude Code **compacts** the conversation into a summary. The summary keeps your requests and key code, but detailed instructions from early in the conversation may be lost. A new session starts with a fresh window.
outputs: The context for each model request

components.label: Permission check
components.summary: Decides, before a tool runs, whether to run it, ask you, or refuse. Deny rules, ask rules, and allow rules are checked in that order.
components.explanation:
The result depends on the **permission mode** and on your rules.

- **Manual**: asks before file edits and shell commands.
- **Accept edits**: edits files and runs common filesystem commands without asking.
- **Plan**: explores and proposes a plan without editing your source files.
- **Auto**: a classifier reviews actions and blocks the risky ones.

The prompt shows the exact action. If you choose "don't ask again", Claude Code saves a rule for that command, and that record stops the question from coming back. The lesson shows why an approval must belong to one exact version of an action.

references.label: Configure permissions
references.note: Rules are evaluated in order: deny, then ask, then allow.

components.label: Tools
components.summary: The actions Claude can take: read and edit files, search, run shell commands, and fetch from the web.
components.explanation:
The built-in tools fall into five groups: file operations, search, execution, web, and code intelligence.

Each tool call returns information that goes back into the context. That result decides what the model proposes next.
outputs: A result: file text, search matches, or command output

references.path: Claude Code docs: How Claude Code works

components.label: Your repository and terminal
components.summary: The files, git state, and commands that tools act on. This is where the change lands.
components.explanation: Before Claude edits a file, Claude Code snapshots it, so you can rewind with `Esc` twice. These checkpoints cover file changes only. They cannot undo actions on remote systems.

references.label: How Claude Code works
references.path: Claude Code docs: How Claude Code works

components.label: Hooks
components.summary: Your own scripts that run at set moments, such as before or after a tool call. A hook can block a call.
components.explanation:
A hook is a handler that runs at an event, for example `PreToolUse` or `Stop`. A command hook reads the event as JSON and can block the action with exit code 2.

A hook can deny a call, but a hook that says nothing does not approve it.
inputs: Event details such as the tool name and its input

references.label: Hooks reference
references.note: Hook events, exit codes, and PreToolUse decisions.

components.label: Subagents
components.summary: Helpers that work in their own context window and send back only a summary.
components.explanation:
A subagent has its own system prompt, its own tool access, and its own permissions. Its many file reads stay out of your main context.

Built-in subagents include Explore, which searches the codebase read-only, and Plan.

components.label: MCP servers and skills
components.summary: MCP servers connect Claude to outside tools and data. Skills are reusable instructions that load only when used.
components.explanation:
**MCP** stands for Model Context Protocol. A server can run as a local process or be reached over HTTP. Its tools appear next to the built-in tools, and the permission check covers them too. Tool definitions load on demand, so they cost little context until Claude uses one.

A **skill** is a SKILL.md file with a description and instructions. Claude sees the description, and the full text loads into the context only when the skill is used. You can run one yourself with `/skill-name`.
inputs: A tool call for an outside service

references.label: Extend Claude with skills
references.note: Descriptions load at start. Full content loads when used.

items.text: The walkthroughs assume Manual mode, where Claude asks before file edits and shell commands. Other modes ask less, and Auto mode lets a classifier decide.
Which rules in your project must always hold? Memory files are context, so a rule like that needs a hook or a deny rule.
The exact point where compaction starts, and what the summary keeps, are not stated in the pages this board draws on.

scenarios.title: Fix a failing test
scenarios.summary: One pass through the loop, from your prompt to a change in your files.

steps.caption: You ask Claude to fix a failing test. Memory files were loaded into the context at the start of the session.
The harness sends the context to the model. The model proposes a tool call: run the tests.
The permission check sees a shell command. In Manual mode it asks you, and you approve.
The tool runs the tests in your terminal. The failure output goes back into the context.
The model proposes an edit. After approval, the tool changes the file in your repository.
The loop runs the tests again to verify. It ends when they pass, and Claude reports back to you.

scenarios.title: You refuse a command
scenarios.summary: A call that does not pass the permission check never runs.

steps.caption: The model proposes a shell command that deletes files.
The permission check asks you. A matching deny rule would refuse the call before it asks.
You refuse. The tool does not run, and your files stay as they were.
What Claude does next is not described on this board. See the open item about refusals.

scenarios.title: A long session fills the context
scenarios.summary: Why rules that matter belong in memory files and not in your first message.

steps.caption: File contents and command output keep arriving in the context window.
Near the limit, Claude Code compacts the conversation into a summary.
Detailed instructions from early in the conversation may be lost in the summary.
Rules in a CLAUDE.md file are context that Claude Code loads at the start of a session, so put persistent rules there.

scenarios.title: Hooks, helpers, and outside tools
scenarios.summary: How the four extension points join the loop.

steps.caption: A hook runs before a tool call. It blocks a command that you never want to run.
A subagent searches the codebase in its own context window.
Only a short summary comes back, so your main context stays small.
An MCP server adds a tool that reads from an outside service. The permission check covers it too.
A skill adds its instructions to the context only when it is used.
